doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

chapter: Studio work, recordings and Saturday Night Live
title: Where he fits among trombonists; wider intervals and alternate positions
summary: He declines to rank himself, praises Tommy Dorsey, Lawrence Brown and others, and describes his wide intervals from Woody Shaw and alternate positions from Lester Young.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: You sound like a modest man as far as how you think about your own playing. And if you could set that modesty aside for a moment, where do you think you fall in the list of influential trombone players?

It’s not for me to say. Everybody has a different take. You know I mean there are some people that think Tommy Dorsey was the greatest ever and as a balladeer for that style of playing that he kind of evolved from listening to Lawrence Brown. He’s got Lawrence Brown. Because Lawrence Brown used many types of vibrato. Sometimes he’d use a lip vibrato, sometimes he’d use a slide vibrato. And they used to run up to the Cotton Club to see Duke and all that and caught that ball and ran with it and made it his whole thing. And he perfected it. He was smooth as silk. And he wasn’t on a mic either. All the guys that played that way in recent years, they play real soft and the put the mic right in the bell of the horn. Tommy — I’ve got video of Tommy man, he’s three feet from the mic and you can hear the sound full, it’s just singing over the band. But anyway, he wasn’t a real improviser. Not really you know. He was okay but that wasn’t his forte. His forte was ballads. But everybody got a different take on it. Then some people like Kid Ory, I love them all. Some people like, you know, Lawrence Brown, or they might like J.J. or Curtis or Julian Priester or Frank Rossolino. I love them all. You know they’re all doing something different. They’re all unique. So you know I’ve got a unique thing that I do and I have my influences and we’re all coming out of something before us for the most part. But I use wider intervals. I started using fourths and fifths to make lines. And I got that from Woody Shaw. He showed me how to do that. So I create melodies and lines out of wider intervals. I also did a thing, I was the first to do this sound on the trombone where I use alternate positions [scats] because I was listening to Lester Young and he used alternate fingerings on the same note [scats] you know so I go [scats] and I was trying to do that but it didn’t come out quite the same but it had a sound so I took that ball and ran with it, and now a lot of guys are copying that. going back to 1970. And of course the shells. I brought that to jazz [inaudible]. People can judge it how they want. That’s not my care. I don’t really care, it’s not why I’m doing it.
